4	def parse_price(text):
5	    """Parse a price string like "$12.50" or "1,234.50" into a float."""
6	    cleaned = text.strip().lstrip("$")
7	    if "," in cleaned:
8	        # European style decimal comma: "12,50"
9	        cleaned = cleaned.replace(",", ".")
10	    return float(cleaned)

13	def total_value(items):
14	    """Sum price * quantity for (price_text, quantity) pairs."""
15	    return round(sum(parse_price(p) * q for p, q in items), 2)

content.text:
I fixed the bug, and all 5 tests pass: the 4 that were already there plus the new regression test.

`parse_price` in `inventory.py` now treats commas as thousands separators when the string looks like `1,234.50`, `$1,234,567.89` or `1,234,567`. That means a comma followed by exactly three digits, then either a dot or another comma group. Everything else behaves as before, so `"12,50"` is still read as 12.5 and `"12.50"` and `"$3"` are unaffected. I didn't touch `total_value`.

I added `test_thousands_separator` in `tests/test_inventory.py`, covering those three formats.

A bare `"1,234"` (one comma group, no dot) is still read as a European decimal comma, giving 1.234. That follows your rule, since it only counts a comma as a thousands separator when a dot or a second comma group follows.

`tests/` has no `__init__.py`, so `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -t .` fails with an import error. I ran the tests with `PYTHONPATH=. python3 -m unittest tests.test_inventory -v` instead.
